Most of the time, the problem is not the software itself. Errors happen when data is entered incorrectly, salary structures are set up the wrong way, or people forget that automation will process whatever is in the system, whether it is correct or not, and do it quickly. Nigerian businesses need more than just a faster version of their old payroll process. The right payroll automation changes how work is done. What Payroll Automation Actually Does Payroll automation is not just one feature. It handles the entire process, from adding new employees to paying salaries and sending all required deductions to the right authorities. Manual payroll requires people to make decisions at every step, such as checking tax tables, calculating pension amounts, making transfers, and filing PAYE returns. Each step can lead to mistakes, using outdated formulas, or missing deadlines, which causes problems. In an automated workflow, the system manages all the rules. When the NTA 2025 changed the PAYE bands on January 1, 2026, a business with automated payroll only needed to update the system once. A business using spreadsheets had to update everything manually or risk running non-compliant payroll for weeks before noticing. A payroll automation system in Nigeria handles salary calculations for each employee, manages statutory deductions like PAYE, pension, NHF, and NSITF, sends payments to employee accounts, takes care of remittances, creates payslips, and generates payroll reports. It usually starts with small issues that seem easy to fix, until one month when they are not. Payroll should not take more than a day: For a business with 50 employees, manual payroll should not take up three days of the Finance Manager’s month. When it does, that time is lost to financial planning, reporting, and other important work that helps the business grow. You may have seen errors you could not explain: Like a wrong net pay, a deduction that appeared unexpectedly, or an employee being paid twice. If the answer to ‘how did this happen’ is ‘someone changed a formula,’ then the process is not reliable enough to grow with your business. Sometimes, statutory remittances are sent late: PAYE is due by the 10th, pension within seven working days, and NHF every month. When these deadlines are managed manually along with other tasks, they can be missed. Compliance deadlines are handled automatically: The system sends remittances as soon as payroll is processed. A system made for Nigeria updates as soon as the law changes. The system should support your salary structure: Nigerian payroll uses components like basic salary, housing, transport, and allowances, and how these are split affects statutory calculations. articles.summary: 07/09/26 Simpson Strong-Tie Donates $25,000 to the Red CrossFollowing Venezuela Earthquakes Simpson Strong-Tie has donated $25,000 to the American Red Cross in support of relief efforts following the devastating earthquakes in Venezuela on June 24, 2026. The 7.2- and 7.5-magnitude earthquakes have so far claimed the lives of nearly 3,350 people, with close to 50,000 still unaccounted for, while causing structural losses across La Guaira, the capital city of Caracas and several states. The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement has deployed assistance in the affected areas, including 326 volunteers and 62 staff members from the Venezuelan Red Cross. Setting up a field hospital and first aid stations, distributing humanitarian aid, providing shelter, and family reunification are among the immediate priority support actions underway. “The images coming out of Venezuela over the last several days have been extremely heartbreaking to see; our thoughts are with the Venezuelan people as they deal with this overwhelming tragedy,” said Simpson Strong-Tie President and CEO Mike Olosky. “As search-and-rescue efforts continue, we’re grateful to the Red Cross and Red Crescent for their swift and dedicated response on the ground and across their network.” Along with the initial donation, Simpson Strong-Tie is matching employee donations up to a total of $5,000 per year. This contribution reflects the company’s ongoing commitment to aid in disaster relief and recovery efforts around the world. To donate, visit www.redcross.org.

articles.summary: What is the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)? Cyber Resilience Act What is the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)? The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is a European Union regulation that establishes mandatory cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, including hardware, software, and connected devices. The CRA aims to ensure products are secure by design, supported throughout their lifecycle, and better protected against evolving cyber threats. Why CRA Matters The growing number of connected products has increased the need for stronger cybersecurity protections. The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) helps address this challenge by establishing common cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements placed on the EU market. The regulation improves transparency, strengthens product security throughout the lifecycle, and helps organizations and consumers make more informed technology decisions. Proliferation of Connected Products Billions of devices across industries and homes Growing Cyber Threats Real-world attacks exploiting unpatched and insecure products Market Gaps Inconsistent security, no transparency, limited lifecycle support Regulatory Response The EU Cyber Resilience Act establishes mandatory cybersecurity requirements EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) Timeline The Cyber Resilience Act is being introduced in stages, with key milestones leading up to full applicability in December 2027. The timeline below outlines the major dates organizations should be aware of as they prepare for CRA compliance. CRA Scope – What Is Covered? CRA Scope – What Is Covered? The Cyber Resilience Act applies to a broad range of products with digital elements, including hardware, software, components, and certain remote services. While many connected products fall within the scope of the regulation, some categories—such as standalone cloud or SaaS services, non-commercial open-source software, products covered by equivalent sector regulations, and other exclusions defined by EU legislation—are not subject to CRA requirements. Hardware SoCs & Processors Microcontrollers IoT Devices Network Equipment Consumer Electronics Industrial Devices Software Firmware Operating Systems Applications Middleware Security Software Embedded Software Components Hardware Components Software Components Firmware Modules Embedded Modules Components Remote Data Processing Solutions (covered when necessary for the product to perform one or more of its intended functions) Both final products and their components are in scope. Hardware and software components are considered Products with Digital Elements (PDE) under the CRA. Secure Biometric Authentication Secure fingerprint sensors engineered for speed and accuracy. Hardware-based authentication replaces passwords with seamless, enterprise-grade protection—enabling fast login and trusted security across modern notebook designs. Standalone Cloud / SaaS Pure cloud services or SaaS offerings not necessary for the product to perform its intended functions. Non-commercial Open Source Free and open-source software projects not supplied in the course of a commercial activity. Equivalent Sector Regulations Medical Devices, Automotive, Civil Aviation, and Maritime products and systems. Other Exclusions Defined by EU Legislation If specific products are sufficiently covered by existing EU cybersecurity legislation. CRA Applicability – New vs. Existing Products CRA Applicability – New vs. Existing Products Which Products does the CRA apply to? Starting December 11, 2027 , new products with digital elements placed on the EU market must comply with the Cyber Resilience Act. Products already on the market before that date are generally exempt unless they undergo a substantial modification that impacts cybersecurity requirements or changes the product's intended purpose. When significant changes are made, a compliance reassessment may be required.
